      Hernia? Consider Robotic Repair

      Outpatient approach offers less risk of complications and speedier recoveries
      By Roy Cummings
      on October 07, 2026

      JORDAN PYSZ / VOLUSIA HEALTH CARE NEWS
      David’s plans to visit the only four states he hasn’t been to were interrupted by a hernia, but that was repaired with robotic assistance at AdventHealth.

      Listen to audio version of this article
      Sponsored by
      0:00 / 3:02
      Instaread

      At the end of what he describes as an “eclectic working career,” one in which he worked an assembly line for General Motors, was CEO of a nonprofit and did some consulting work, David James mentored children in need at Holly Hill Middle School.

      “It was a wonderful opportunity to work with some students who had made some less than desirable choices, and to see them respond to relationship, relevance and resilience was one of the most meaningful things I’ve done,” David says.

      That’s saying a lot because David, 74, has done a lot. He’s traveled extensively around the world and domestically to all but four of the 50 US states. He was hoping to get to those four states this year, but a double inguinal hernia forced a change of plans.

      Most commonly affecting the abdomen or groin area, a hernia occurs whenever an organ or the fatty tissue around it squeezes through a weak spot in the surrounding muscle wall or connective tissue.

      David first suffered a hernia when he was a child, and while there are now several ways in which a hernia can be repaired, the one thing that has not changed in all those years is that a hernia still must be repaired surgically.

      For that, David turned to board-certified general surgeon, Gregory Burgoyne, MD, of AdventHealth Medical Group, who recommended robotic surgery over open or laparoscopic surgery because its minimally invasive nature offers advantages for both the patient and surgeon.

      “Robotic surgery allows us to repair the hernia by using tools that are inserted into the body through three tiny incisions that are each less than a centimeter long,” the doctor explains.

      The tools include a 3D camera and two or three interactive robotic arms. The camera provides the physician with a clear view of the surgical area on a monitor. The doctor uses the robotic arms to push the protruding tissue back into place and reinforce the abdominal wall.

      “A lot of people have questions about the robot because they think it’s controlled by artificial intelligence, but that’s not accurate,” Dr. Burgoyne says. “The robot is simply a tool that I control.”

      With this approach, even complex hernia surgery becomes an outpatient procedure rather than one requiring an overnight hospital stay.

      It also reduces the risk of wound infection and shortens patient recovery time. David, for example, was “back to normal” two weeks after surgery.

      “And I was only on the pain meds they gave me for two days,” he adds. “After that, I didn’t need them.

      “When I went back for my two-week follow-up after surgery, Dr. Burgoyne told me everything looked great and that I probably wouldn’t need to come back to see him.”

      “It was a really good experience, and with Dr. Burgoyne and his staff, I just got this feeling that they were going to take good care of me.

      “They have a kindness about them that I call service with care, and so I would absolutely recommend them.”

      Gregory B. Burgoyne, MD

      Laparoscopy Surgery
      is a board-certified general surgeon specializing in hernia repair, complex hernia, abdominal wall reconstruction, open and laparoscopic surgery and endoscopy. Read more...
